title: MUF, LUF and propagation paths
blurb: Explain the usable frequency window between LUF and MUF, how far one hop reaches, and short versus long path.

G3B01.why: Short and long path signals both arrive, and the long one is later, so you hear a **slightly delayed echo**.
G3B01.trap: Nothing makes it fade on a fixed 10-second cycle or add 3 dB.

G3B02.why: The MUF depends on sunlight (time, season), solar radiation, disturbances and the **specific path**: all of them.

G3B03.why: Absorption falls as frequency rises, so the least loss is **just below the MUF**, the highest frequency still refracted.
G3B03.trap: Just above the LUF is where absorption is still greatest.

G3B04.why: A network of **automated receiving stations** shows where your signal is actually being heard right now.
G3B04.trap: The A-index describes Earth's field, not your path.

G3B05.why: Between the LUF and MUF the ionosphere **refracts the wave back to Earth**.

G3B06.why: Below the LUF, absorption wins: the signal is **attenuated before reaching** the destination.
G3B06.trap: Passing through the ionosphere is what happens above the MUF.

G3B07.why: LUF is the **Lowest Usable Frequency** for communication between two specific points.

G3B08.why: MUF is the **Maximum Usable Frequency** between two points. Above it, waves pass through.

G3B09.why: The F2 region is the highest, so one hop reaches about **2,500 miles**.

G3B10.why: The E region is lower, so a single hop reaches about **1,200 miles**.

G3B11.why: With no frequency above the LUF yet below the MUF, the **window is closed** and ordinary skywave can't work.

G3B12.why: Lower HF bands in summer suffer **high atmospheric noise**: thunderstorm static.
G3B12.trap: Lower bands still propagate. Static is the problem, not absorption by photons.
